result.summary: The Chorus of Ocean's daughters laments Prometheus's punishment, and he explains how he lifted mankind from ignorance by teaching them crafts, medicine, prophecy and mining. He hints that Fate, not Zeus, rules, and that a secret will eventually free him.

scenes.title: The Chorus laments
scenes.summary: The Chorus mourns Prometheus and says the whole world, from Asia to the sea and Hades, shares his pain.
scenes.stakes: Prometheus suffers eternal punishment by Zeus; the Chorus grieves and fears Zeus's harsh rule.

scenes.title: Prometheus lists his gifts
scenes.summary: Prometheus explains how he gave humans reason, building, astronomy, numbers, letters, taming animals, medicine, prophecy and metals.
scenes.stakes: He remains bound in torment despite all he gave mankind.

scenes.title: Fate and the secret
scenes.summary: The Chorus hopes he will be freed; Prometheus says Necessity, steered by the Fates and Furies, binds even Zeus, and he refuses to reveal his secret.
scenes.stakes: His eventual release depends on keeping his secret hidden from Zeus.

notable_quotes.reason: Prometheus sums up his claim as culture-giver: every human art comes from him.
Memorable statement that craft is weaker than Necessity.

analysis.text: Prometheus portrays himself as civilization's founder, setting human progress against Zeus's tyranny and the limits fate places on all power.
The catalogue of arts reflects Greek ideas of progress from primitive life, including divination, which was central to Greek religion.

legacy.text: The figure of Prometheus as bringer of civilization influenced Romantic writers such as Shelley in Prometheus Unbound (1820).

fun_facts.text: The passage in sentence 8 is bracketed in the translation because scholars doubt its authenticity as part of the original text.

language_notes.text: "Gods of eld" means the gods of old, the older Titan generation that Zeus has displaced.
The fearless maidens of Colchis are the Amazons, warrior women; Colchis lies on the Black Sea's eastern shore. The Maeotic lake is the Sea of Azov.
"Mellay" is an old form of melee, a confused hand-to-hand fight.
Atlas, a Titan, was punished by Zeus by being made to hold up the sky. The bracketed text is marked as of doubtful authenticity.
Prometheus reminds the Chorus that he helped Zeus win power and fixed the privileges of each new god; "upstart" is his scornful term for them.
"Flaxen-winged car" is a poetic phrase for a ship with linen sails.
A "leech" is an old word for a physician.
This describes divination: reading omens from bird flight and from the entrails, gall, liver and burnt thigh-bones of sacrificed animals.
"Beyond due measure" means excessively; the Chorus warns Prometheus that his kindness to humans went too far and cost him dearly.
"Forasmuch as" is an archaic phrase meaning "since" or "because"; "loosed" means freed.
"Not thus, nor yet" means: not in this way, and not yet. Fate's fulfilment of his release will come later and only after suffering.
"Art" here means craft or skill, including Prometheus' own cunning, not fine art.
"Triform" means three-shaped, referring to the three Fates; the Furies are "mindful" because they remember wrongs and punish them.
"Importunate" means persistently pressing; Prometheus tells the Chorus to stop pushing him for the secret.
"In no wise meet time" means it is not at all a fitting time; "bethink ye" means consider or think of.

context_notes.text: The Chorus are the Oceanids, sea-nymph daughters of Oceanus, who have come to sympathise with the chained Prometheus.
Prometheus here claims writing and number as his gifts. Aeschylus lists the civilising arts that set humans apart from their primitive state.
The Fates (Moirai) spun and ended each life's destiny; the Furies (Erinyes) punished crimes such as broken oaths and offences against kin. Together they stand above even the gods.
Prometheus' secret concerns a threat to Zeus's rule, which he knows through his foresight. Zeus later wants it, and its disclosure is his bargaining power.

literary_notes.text: Waves, the deep, Hades and rivers all lament, making the whole natural world share Prometheus's grief.
Early humans are compared to swarming ants living in sunless caves, stressing their helpless, mindless state.
The giver of every human skill has no skill to free himself, a bitter reversal.
Prometheus is likened to a poor doctor who cannot cure himself, though he taught medicine to humans.
This closing summary claims all human art for Prometheus, and its blunt, compressed form gives it the force of a boast.
The short, general maxim sets human and divine cleverness below necessity, giving the scene its theme: even Prometheus' skill is limited.
Necessity is imagined as a ship with a steersman, making abstract fate seem like a guided vessel and prompting the question of who controls it.
The Chorus assumes Zeus's destiny is simply eternal rule, while Prometheus knows otherwise, so the audience senses a hidden threat to Zeus's power.
Prometheus links his escape to guarding the secret, hinting at a future conflict with Zeus and his eventual release.
